extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists, legal scholars and practitioners interested in the Espionage Act, leaks, and related prosecutions
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of how the U.S. Espionage Act has been applied historically and in recent decades, summarizing the statutory provisions charged, notable cases, prosecutorial practices, criticisms, and consequences for leaks and disclosures to the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the Espionage Act to disclosures to the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how the Espionage Act applies to disclosures of classified or national defense information to journalists and news organizations — an issue described as 'not entirely clear' and litigated in test cases such as Morison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Morison prosecution was used as a broader campaign against leaks as a 'test case' for applying the Act to disclosure to the press. Commentary (Time) framed the tension: 'The Government does need to protect military secrets, the public does need information to judge defense policies, and the line between the two is surpassingly difficult to draw.' The page documents multiple prosecutions and indictments involving communication with the press (e.g., Sterling, Drake, Kim, Snowden, Risen-related matters), showing practical application even where statutory boundaries are debated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized communication of national defense information
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal offense language charged as 'unauthorized communication of national defense information' and 'willful communication of classified intelligence with an unauthorized person'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in high-profile prosecutions such as the charges against Edward Snowden (charged with 'unauthorized communication of national defense information' and 'willful communication of classified intelligence with an unauthorized person'). The element focuses on communication to an unauthorized recipient, regardless of motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful retention and transmission of national defense information
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful retention and/or transmission of national defense information (a felony offense), charged where an individual knowingly retains classified material and transmits it or allows it to be transmitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Reality Leigh Winner (charged with 'willful retention and transmission of national defense information' and sentenced to five years and three months) and Daniel Hale (pleaded guilty to unlawful retention and transmission). The wording highlights both the willfulness element and the transmission/retention conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful retention/possession of classified documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution for willfully retaining classified documents in one's possession, even without proven dissemination to a foreign power or the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases include Kenneth Wayne Ford Jr. (indicted under 18 U.S.C. § 793(e) for having a box of documents post-employment), Robert L. Birchum (retired Lt.Col sentenced for unlawfully possessing and retaining classified documents), and aspects of the Trump indictment (31 counts of willful retention of national defense information). Sentencing can be severe even without proof of dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theft of government property as an attendant offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges of theft of government property may accompany Espionage Act counts where classified materials were taken or retained improperly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: John Walker's case partner Morison was convicted on counts of espionage and two counts of theft of government property. Theft charges can be used alongside espionage charges to capture property-based misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 U.S.C. § 793 — disclosure/retention by persons with unauthorized possession (subsections d/e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions under § 793 (notably subsections (d) and (e)) used to charge disclosure to reporters or willful retention of national defense information by employees/contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stephen Jin-Woo Kim (indicted under § 793(d) for alleged disclosure to a reporter), Kenneth W. Ford Jr. (§ 793(e)), Thomas Drake (indicted under § 793(e) for alleged willful retention). The statute has been applied to both transmission to unauthorized persons and unlawful retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 U.S.C. § 794 — spying for a foreign power (subsections a/c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions criminalizing espionage for a foreign power (e.g., § 794(a), § 794(c)), used in classic spy prosecutions involving transmission of classified information to adversary states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable convictions under § 794 include Aldrich Ames (§ 794(c)) and other Cold War-era spy cases. The section has been used in prosecutions where disclosure was to a foreign government (e.g., Soviets/Russia) rather than to the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 U.S.C. § 798(a)(3) — disclosure of classified information (special categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute criminalizing unauthorized disclosure of classified information relating to communications intelligence and certain protected categories (used against translators or those handling particularly sensitive material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shamai Leibowitz pleaded guilty under 18 U.S.C. § 798(a)(3) after admitting to sharing information with a blogger; Leibowitz was sentenced pursuant to a plea bargain. Section 798 has been used in contexts involving classified intelligence and translators/analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conspiracy to obtain and disseminate classified information (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 793(g) and related conspiracy counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging conspiracy to unlawfully obtain and/or disseminate classified information — applied in cases involving organized efforts to acquire and publish classified material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Julian Assange was charged/pleaded guilty to a conspiracy charge (violation of 18 U.S.C. § 793(g) in the referenced agreement) relating to seeking and disseminating classified information. Conspiracy counts can target coordination between sources and publishers or intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the Espionage Act beyond 'traditional espionage' (prosecutorial expansion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of applying the Espionage Act to cases that do not involve spying for a foreign power but instead involve withholding information or communicating with the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that under the Obama and first Trump administrations at least eight prosecutions were related not to traditional espionage but to withholding information or communicating with members of the press; out of eleven prosecutions against government officials for providing classified information to the press, seven occurred since Obama took office. This demonstrates prosecutorial trends expanding the Act's use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of a public-interest defense / limits on defense arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical and legal limits preventing defendants accused under the Espionage Act from presenting public-interest justifications, First Amendment defenses, or argument about over-classification at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commentators and practitioners (Daniel Ellsberg, Trevor Timm, Jesselyn Radack) argue that defendants cannot effectively present a public-interest defense and often cannot raise First Amendment arguments or testify about motives tied to exposing wrongdoing. Trevor Timm: 'basically any information the whistleblower or source would want to bring up at trial to show that they are not guilty... the jury would never hear.' The lack of an accepted public-interest defense is a central criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms of overbreadth, chilling effect, and prosecutorial tool use
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative judgments that the Espionage Act is 'too blunt', 'aggressive, broad and suppressive', and causes chilling effects on speech, whistleblowing, and press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited sources: a 2015 PEN America study quoting experts calling the Act 'too blunt an instrument' and 'a tool of intimidation'; legal scholars (e.g., Stephen Vladeck) arguing the law 'lacks the hallmarks of a carefully and precisely defined statutory restriction on speech.' Daniel Ellsberg and others have urged Supreme Court review. These critiques inform debates about reform (e.g., calls for a public-interest defense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial strategy as deterrence and warnings to the press
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of prosecutions or public threats of prosecution to deter publication of leaked information and to signal to news organizations the costs of publishing classified material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CIA Director William J. Casey in 1986 threatened to prosecute five news organizations without citing specific violations; the Morison prosecution was used as a 'test case' to warn against publication of leaked information. The page documents how prosecutions serve both legal and political deterrent functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity of penalties and sentencing outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Espionage Act and related statutes can produce severe sentences (long prison terms, long supervised release) for convictions even in leak-related cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable sentencing examples: Morison sentenced to two years (1985); Chelsea Manning convicted on six counts and originally sentenced to 35 years (later commuted to ~7 years served); Harold T. Martin sentenced to nine years (2017); Reality Winner sentenced to five years and three months (described as longest for unauthorized release to media at time); Robert L. Birchum sentenced to three years; Trump faced multiple willful retention counts (case developments detailed). These examples show significant sentencing exposure.
